Only Indians That Can DoIt.
saw Geronimo and dozen of his
| Apaches do something in Arizona in
1887 which / never would have believed
| possible had / not witnessed it with my
own eyes.


The Apaches are unquestionably the
most dreaded tribe of Indians on the
continent. They are tougher, more en-
during and more unconquerable than
any other of their race. An Apache can
lope up the side of a mountain with the
thermometer marking 100 degs., and
when he reaches the top he won't show
drop of extra perspiration, nor will he
breathe q whit faster than when he
started.


He will go for days without a morsel
Of food OF drop of water; he will live
On snakes, mice and refuse, or, if the
worst comes to the worst, will shoot his
horse and eat what he wants of him raw
Bet out to pursue band of Apache raid
ers, and if they are hard pressed they
will separate, each for himself, so that
the only way to keep up the pursuit is
to follow them individually, in which
case the Apache is sure to have the best
end of the contract. When the hunt is
over the dusky miscreants will come to-
yether at some point twenty or thirty or
more miles away.


There were twenty-five of us cavalry
men returning from one of our fruitless
pursuits If the terrible Geronimo. Our
horses were worn out, and so were we.
1t was one of the hottest days l have
ever known in that throbbing furnace
Of country. We had several miles Of
baked alkali plain still to traverse before
reaching the fort, where we could secure
shade and water, and what we needed
most of all-rest.


Whew! but it was hotl Had not the
air been perfectly dry neither man nor
beast could have stood it. The metal
one could bear to touch it with the
naked hand. The air shimmered and
throbbed as it does over newly plowed
field at noontide of summer day.


North, east, south and west was one
level stretch of plain, on which not a
tree, shrub or even blade of grass grew.
Far to the westward could be seen the
outlines of the fort, oddly distorted
through the quivering atmosphere, but
-. <>tl ~ -
burning desert.


We were strung along for distance of
several hundred yards. In fact there was
q squad of five horsemen much farther
than that in the rear. All the animals
were plodding slowly through the sand,
which it seemed to me was hot enough
to roast eggs, their heads dropping,
while we were simply enduring it, grim
ly closing our teeth, holding out to reach
the post.


Was there anything to be apprehended
from Geronimo? Could we old cam
paigners be entrapped? Low, level sands
on every hand. Well, right there in the
midst of that flaming plain, with its
horrible sandy waste, in which no spear
of grass could find root, that frightful
;hieftain and his Apaches ambuscaded
as. 1t sounds incredible, but it is fact.


Suddenly l heard rifle firing at the
rear. 1t had a dull, odd sound, but it
was close at hand, and as turned in
the saddle saw that the squad farthest
away were engaged in desperate fight
with party of Indians, who were ON
foot, shooting, striking and darting
hither and thither like so many demons.


We instantly wheeled and hurried
back as fast as we could to the help Of
our comrades, but before we could reach
them three saddles were emptied, and
Geronimo and his warriors were scurry-
ing across the plain at greater speed
than any to which we could force our
exhausted ponies, who sank to- their fet-
locks at every step. We gave them
parting volley, which wounded several,
but they managed to limp off with the
help of others, and all were soon beyond
danger. l don't know how far they
travelled off over that burning desola-
ton, but it may have been many miles,
for they were capable of doing it if they
chose.


These Apaches must have discovered
our approach while we were good way
off. Knowing we were on our return to
the post they could easily calculate
where we would pass. Then they bur-
rowed in the sand, covering themselves
entirely with the blistering particles, so
that only their snakelike eyes peered
forth. Thus we passed within a few
rods of them without suspeuting their
presence.


In conversation with General Crook
about the extraordinary incident, that
old campaigner smiled and replied:


81 am not surprised. have seen them
do the same thing myself, but the
Apache is the only Indian that can do
it."-Chicago Mail.

danger. I don't know how far they
travelled off over that burning desola-
tion, but it may have been many miles,
for they were capable of doing it if they
chose.


These Apaches must have discovered
our approach while we were a good way
off. Knowing we were on our return to
the post they could easily calculate
where we would pass. Then they bur-
rowed in the sand, covering themselves
entirely with the blistering particles, so
that only their snakelike eyes peered
forth. Thus we passed within a few
rods of them without suspecting their
presence.


In conversation with General Crook
about the extraordinary incident, that
old campaigner smiled and replied:


"I am not surprised. I have seen them
do the same thing myself, but the
Apache is the only Indian that can do
it."—Chicago Mail.

lowing experience of Mr. William Black.

patches are pouring in from all direc-
tions asking if the men on the Atlantic
division of the Canadian Pacific
railway intend to strike in sympa-
thy with the train hands in the west.
Conductor Cassidy, representative

that there will be no strike in this sec-
tion. The western strikers have not
even sent word asking sympathy. The
men here say the company has dealt
honestly with them. A number of men
have been sent from here to Manitoba to
take the places of the strikers.

the probate court received a singular
letter today. It was dated "Cell No. 80,
stone, San Quentin Prison, California"
and protested against permitting the
will of Alonzo Wood being carried into
effect. The letter is signed Frederick
Lansing Wood, and declares that the
will is the elimination of conspiracy
lasting through a series of years.

leaving an estate of $4,000. An exam-
ination of the will brings to light a clause
disinheriting his son Frederick, described
as having been given more opportunities
than any of the testator's other children,
and yet he repeatedly threatened the
life of his father. The son, according
to the will, is in prison for murder.

BROOKLYN, April 17.—Being Easter

them was on the front of the pulpit and
wreaths of them over the pulpit. The

was added to the great congregational
singing. Text, Samuel XIV. 5, "Surely
the bitterness of death is past."

So cried Agag, and the only objection
to this text is that a bad man ut-
tered it. Nevertheless, it is true, and
it has a higher and better sense than that in
which it was originally uttered. Years
ago a legend something like this was
told me: In a hut lived a very poor
woman by the name of Misery. In front
of her door was a pear tree, which was
her only resource for a living. Christ

came through the earth and no one would en-
tertain him. In vain he knocked at the
door of palaces and of humble dwell-
ings. Cold and hungry and insufficiently
clad, as he was, none received him.
But coming one day to the hut of this
woman, whose name was Misery, she
received him and offered him a few
crusts and asked him to warm himself
at the handful of coals, and she sat by
all night that the wayfarer might have a
pillow to rest on.

In the morning this divine being asked
her as he departed what she would have
him do in the way of reward, and told
her that he owned the universe and
would give her what she asked. All she
asked was that her pear tree might be
protected, and that the boys who stole
her fruit, once climbing the tree, might
not be able to get down without her con-
sent. So it was granted, and all who
climbed the tree were compelled to stay
there. After a while Death came along
and told the poor woman she must go
with him. But she did not want to go,
for, however poor one is, no one
wants to go with Death. Then she said
to Death, "I will go with you if you
first climb up into my pear tree and
bring me down a few pears before
I start." This he consented to do, but
having climbed into the tree he could
not again come down.

Then the troubles of the world began
for Death did not come. The physician
had no patients, the undertakers no bus-
iness, lawyers no wills to make, the peo-
ple who waited for inheritances could
not get them, the old men staid in all
the professions and occupations, so that
there was no room for the young who
were coming on, and the earth got over-
crowded, and from all the earth the cry
went up: "Oh, for Death. Where is
Death?" Then the people came to the
poor woman and begged her to let Death
descend from the tree. In sympathy for

come down on one condition, and that
was that he should never molest or take

with us.

our divine permission to quit it. Sixty

planet. Thirty million people every
year board this planet. As a steamer

cargo, and as the passengers of a rail
train must leave it in order to have an

it is with this world.

happen to a rail train if one who pur-

seat assigned him? And what would

into it never departed from it? The
grave is as much benediction as the
cradle. What sunk that ship in the

passengers. What was the matter with
that steamer on the Thames which, a
few years ago, went down with 60 lives:

world is only a ship, which was launched
some six thousand years ago. It is sail-

tions? The men and women who started
when the world started would keep the
modern people back and down, saying,

down. History is nothing, for we are
older than history." What mercy for
the human race was death. Within
a few years you can get from this world
all there is in it.

seventy springtimes, you have seen
enough blossoms. After fifty or sixty,

or sixty or seventy winters, you have
seen enough snowstorms and felt enough
chills and wrapped yourself in enough
blankets. In the ordinary length of a
man's life you have carried enormous
burdens, and shed enough tears, and suf-
fered enough injustices, and felt enough
pain, and been clouded by enough
depths, and surrounded by enough mys-
teries.

There is danger that the modern
passenger brakeman will die of ennui.
On the Fort Wayne road there is
now in process of testing device
which is to be operated by COM
pressed air from the engineers cab,
and which is, in effect, noiseless
annunciator, quietly informing the
passengers, through their eyes, not
their ears, of the name of the next
stopping place. This, if generally
adopted, will rob the brakeman of
the dear joy of shouting in an un-
known tongue. One by one of this
officials duties have passed away.
A decade ago he twisted the hand
brake as vigorously, and oftener, than
his co-worker on the freight train.
Air and the engineer now perform
that arduous duty. Now comes the
silent, air-operated station annuncia-
tor. There are few privileges, how
ever, left to the passenger brakeman,
which the man in the engine cannot
take away. There are pretty girls
to help on and off, fat women, babies,
old men and packages unnumbered
to look after. But the vocal training
of the brakeman will be totally
neglected, and he will at times sigh
for the days when he could relieve
his feelings by splitting some passen-
gers ear drum and emitting lam
guage that Max Muller himself could
not interpret.-Pitsbarg Bulletin.

Lael was employed by the St. Louis,
Iron Mountain and Southern railroad
company as caller and was on duty
last night. He ran into one of the
saloons, where Wear pursued him,
thence to the company's yards in the
lower part of town, where, for a time,
he escaped from Wear. In the encounter he lost his hat in the street
and requested some of the employees
to go back with him to get it, which
they consented to do. In the mean
time Wear went about the saloons
and depot. Spying Lael on the plat
form of the passenger depot he ap-
preached him, and quickly drawing
a revolver leveled it at Lael's head
and fired. Two or three of Lael's
friends were near him at the time, but
as Wear was not carrying any cane or
crutch they had no idea that any serious trouble would result. Lael threw
up his hand to ward off the weapon,
but was too late. He fell mortally
wounded.

brought out by the coroner's inquest,
held yesterday. Lael was about 81
years of age, innocuous, and bore a
good reputation. He was married less
than a year, and his widow, who is in
a delicate condition, is almost crushed
over the tragedy. Wear, who is in
jail, waived examination.

creased production and a stationary
or diminished demand the price of
some things would fall while that Of
others would rise from opposite con-
ditions.


But these variations would be ad-
justed by the business instincts Of
man. If the price of one thing rose
very much, more people would en-
gage in its production. and the price
would fall to the general level. On
the other hand, if the price of par
Gcular commodity fall, some of the
producers will engage in other pur-
suits, the product will diminish and
the price rise again to the general
level. But where prices are nearly
all falling together it is impossible
for any such adjustment to take
place.


COMMODITIES AND LABOR.


Tt is claimed that commodities
ought to be cheaper now, because it
takes less labor to produce them
That is bad logic, and the economics
of the proposition are still worse.
If it takes less labor to produce a
given commodity, that may be a
good reason why the commodity
should exchange for less labor, but
it is no reason why it should ex-
change for less money. Money and
labor are by no means Identical.


For the money price of commodi-
ties to fall as production increases
would have the effect Of keeping the
producer in the same condition,
while the possessor Of money, and
particularly one who has a large
amount Of it, would realize a great
and uncomfortable advantage.


In this connection | want to read
a brief extract from a speech by
Prof. Taussig, strong advocate Of
the gold standard, recently delivered
before the Liberal Club Of Buffalo,
as reported In the Buffalo Express ::


The fall had been attributed to i'm
proved methods of production, better
machinery and cheaper transportation.
Personally, the speaker had never been
able to find in improved methods of pro-
duCtiOn per Sc any true explanation of
the fall in prices. Commodities had
fallen in price, but there was one crucial
exception to the general tendency,
namely, in regard to mouey incomes
which had not fallen. This was a very
important consideration and put a very
different face on the relations between
debtor and creditor. The former gave
back, it was true, the same amount,
yielding a command over more commod-
tiles. The creditor got more than he
gave, but on the other hand the debtor
had not suffered, his money income was
as large as it was before.


Here is distinct recognition of
three things: First, that prices have
fallen; second, that improved meth
DDS of production, etc., have not been
the cause, and third, that all the
benefit of the change has gone to
the creditor. But he says the debtor
has not been injured. Whether he
has been directly injured or not, he
has a good right to complain, for if
any benefit accrue to the nation as
whole, the debtor surely ought to
receive his share.


Let us take simple illustration
to show how this change will work
between the man who happens to
have money and the producer.


We will suppose community of
.101 persons. One of them has $780,
1000 in money. The other 100 have

San Francisco April 3.—The post office inspectors last week bored to test the foundation, something which ought to have been done weeks ago. It is the only real demonstration of the said foundation. The work done thus far bears out the charge that that portion of the proposed site formed part of a swampy arm of Mission Creek; at the depth of forty feet boggy ooze was struck and below this were sand and water. The usual formation on the low lands of this peninsula is hard sand, which makes an admirable foundation. Such sand is under the Chronicle building and the now Crocker building. The borings on this post office site show that the soil has been made by washings of sand and clay from the bay and is not natural formation. It is not to be supposed that the Government will wish to go down sixty or seventy feet to obtain secure foundation on its lot, which is exceedingly costly. It stands.

This post office controversy has revived the curious proceedings of the commission which was appointed by Secretary Interior in 1857. The original commissioners were John P. Irish, W. J. Bryan and H. Stone. Stone soon resigned and J. X. MaSten was appointed in his place. Of these, Irish and MaSten were resident of Oakland. How would New Yorkers relish two Brooklyn men out of the three members of a commission to select for them a site for US public building? The commission were also required by law to select sites in the order of desirability and to submit the list to Washington; they never did this but chose one site tonight for it, and when it was rejected, elected another. They never made choice of a site that the first news San Francisco received about it came from Washington. This explains why no local protests were sent at the time the selection of the site was made.

Another heavy storm this week brought abundant rain in all parts of the state. Counties in the San Joaquin VALLEY getting heavier rainfall than they have enjoyed at one time for years. In the northern part of the state and throughout the Sacramento Valley fully two inches fell, while the average in the southern part was an inch and quarter. The weather in the southern counties is extremely cold considering the time of the season; but the light moss thus far have done little damage.

The reclamation of Timothy Hopkins, treasurer of the Southern Pacific Company, was forestalled when he received $3,000,000 in the compromise of the famous Will contest. To manage properly the large property which he thus acquired will take nearly all his leisure and there added the political clash between the Huntington and Stanford interests over his place. It is accepted as a fact that a nephew of Mr. Huntington will take Hopkins' place as treasurer and will also be coached by General Manager Towns, the attorney's probable successor. It is evident that Mr. Huntington does not propose to relinquish the control of the Southern Pacific, which he acquired by compact with Vail, Eacles, and later with her husband.

The San Francisco Savings Union will soon begin the erection of a new masonry building. It will stand of the old German Savings Bank, adjoining it. When this building is completed, Californians from Monterey to Webb will have an unbroken row of the buildings.

A mad mining excitement is raging in the foothills, about halfway between Los Angeles and San Bernardino. A few miles back of the little town of Lucerne, a prospector struck silver ore, which he says assayed nearly 5000 oz. per ton. Some rich premises were shown in Los Angeles and in the little canyon, the majority being ranchers who wouldn't know good ore if they were to so. The greater part are unprovided with tents and the heavy rains and cold nights have caused recent suffering. The real truth about the camp seems to be that there is a little good but not enough to make it pay than five or ten cents. The other so-called projectors are sure to go back, cursing the men who lured them to a false bonanza. A curious fate of Lucerne is that it is one of the instant towns built at the height of the great land speculation. The large hotel never occupied, but a few years ago it was sold to a colony of Dunkards who converted it into a college. No one man or no man's interest should stand in the way of this reform.

mendations should go out to the elders in the
synod;


Also, That a committee of three be app-
ointed at the close of each topic to report con-
clusions on the discussions. The brother open-
ing the discussion of each to be chairman of
each committee, said reports to be prepared and
submitted at the convenience of the committees
before the adjournment of this body.


The discussion on the next topic, The
Elder and the Prayer Meeting, was
opened by Elder H. L. Hoover, who was
followed by Elders H. B. Norman, W. S.
Summers, and J. H. Byrd.


EDUCATION FOR THE MINISTRY.


The discussion on the topic "Standard
of Education for the Ministry" was
opened by Elders Walter Blair and D.
Humphreys, who held the floor until the
hour for closing the evening session had
arrived.


A motion was made to lay the whole sub-
ject on the table. The motion was opp-
osed, and after a lively discussion, running
late into the hour of recess, indi-
cating that the large majority of the body
desired general discussion on what they
termed "live issue," it was decided that
the discussion should continue and the
body should make an expression upon it.


Night Session.


The night session of the convention was
largely attended, and a number of ladies
were present.


The devotional exercises were conducted
by Ruling Elder J. L. Barbour, after
which the convention resumed its regular
business.


On motion of Ruling Elder James Lyons,
the order providing for the appointment of
committees on topics was rescinded.


The following, offered by Ruling-Elder
H. L. Wexford, Jr., was referred to the
Committee on Business:


Whereas, it is suggested that the Columbian
Exposition, to be held under the patronage of the
United States Government in the city of Chicago
during the next year, should make departure
from hundred and well-established American
precedents in the opening of the exhibition for
public resort upon the Sabbath-day; and where-
as, such departure, in our judgment, will be pro-
ductive of evil and only evil in its proximate and
remotest results; therefore,


Resolved, That we earnestly and most respect-
fully request in the name and on behalf of 20,000
communicants and their families in this
synod, composed in part of three states of the
union, that the authorities in charge of the Ex-
position withhold its gates against the public on
the Sabbath.


And whereas, any contribution from the
United States Treasury must include in part
taxes paid for the support of the government by
20,000,000 of Christian people, of whom the
congregations we represent constitute part;
therefore,


Resolved, That our senators and representa-
tives in Congress be requested to withhold their
assent from any farther appropriation in aid of
the Exposition until assurance be given that it
will not be opened for public visitation upon the
Sabbath day.


TOPICS FURTHER DISCUSSED.


The convention then took up Topic No.
7, "When without a pastor what duty
devolves on the ruling elder as to his
church and people and as to destitute
fields adjacent to his own."


The discussion was opened by Rev. H.
A. Robinson, of the Colley-Memorial
church, and he was followed by Ruling
Elders J. T. Fitzgerald, J. H. Byrd, W. H.
Holman, D. Humphreys, H. B. Norman,
and Rogers.

vated Railroad yard at Third-ave and Ninety-ninth
st., crushed to death under the wheels of a train
yesterday. About twenty minutes before 8 a.m. he jumped the steps of Locomotive No. 225,

was held a witness before the coroner. Morton
twenty-five years old and lived at No. 1664

Recent Testimony of Mountaineers as to

Its Effect on the Human System.

One of the most interesting parts of
Mr. Whymper's new book on his travels
among the Andes of the equator, is
treat of the effect of the rarity of the
air on the human body. Mr. Whymper
has proved scientifically, what thought-
ful mountaineers have asserted, that
with the diminution of atmospheric
pressure goes a diminution of physical
power. He has made a more novel
point by insisting that the human
frame is affected in at least two dis-
tinct ways—one by pressure on the in-
ternal organs from the expansion of
the gases within the body and the
other by the increased exertion re-
quired to inhale sufficient air to feed
the lungs. The first cause creates the
most frequent inconvenience on as-
cents up to 10,000 feet, and the
mountain climber may suffer severely
from it; one week at 1,900 feet
and escape it the next at 4,000 feet,
as it depends largely on the temporary
state of the organs. Mr. Whymper
wrote his book before Mr. Vallot had
made his interesting experiments on
the top of Mount Blanc.

"Three days residence on the top of
Mount Blanc 15,750 feet, sufficed to
entirely modify the method of my
breathing." Mr. Vallot says: "The
last day my pulmonary capacity had
notably augmented. The number of
inspirations was seventeen minute in
place of fourteen in the plain. The
depth of the inspirations was doubled.
Thus, the air being twice less dense
than in the plain, there entered twice
as much air in the lungs and the equi-
librium was thus established. I felt no
symptoms of mountain sickness."

In 1889 Professor Janssen ascended
Mount Blanc. It was the theory of
his that to retain the full use of one's
faculties, mental and bodily, at 10,000
feet, it was necessary to avoid physical
exertion, and as he was to undertake
scientific observations he had himself
up on sled to the top. It is probable
that neither Whymper nor Vallot
would endorse Janssen's theory with
regard to the impairment of the men's
faculties at a lofty elevation. Last
year a lot of workmen had some
rough experience on the top of Mount
Blanc, while they were trying to dig a
tunnel there. Their experience led
them to the conclusion that at the
same time they did one-third less work
than they could do at ordinary levels.

Mr. Freshfield, the well-known
mountaineer, and some other authori-
ties, believe, however, that the lungs
adapt themselves rapidly to new con-
ditions, and the limits of their power
of adaptation must be determined.
The height to be attained by men who
have camped for some time previous
at or above 10,000 feet remains to be
ascertained. Mr. Freshfield says it is
evident that the effect of low atmos-
pheric pressures is modified or intensi-
fied by accidental atmospheric condi-
tions. During the first ascent of Mt.
Elbrus in the Caucasus 15,500 feet,
with six men, nobody was affected con-
sciously by the rarity of the air. Dur-
ing the second ascent all the members
of an equally competent party suffered
more or less. The first party made the
ascent when high wind prevailed and
the other when no breeze was stirring.
The inference is that the high wind
brought plenty of air to the party at
their lofty elevation.

On Monte Rosa, mountain sickness is
very rare. "We cannot but believe,"
M. Freshfield says, "that mountains
which project like promontories above
the lowlands, and up whose slopes rush
draughts of air from the plains, will be
found the best for the attainment of
the highest possible elevations."

Mountaineers now regard the Asiatic
ranges as the best field for the solution
of the question of the effects of rarity
of air upon the human system. It is
important to bear in mind that atmos-
pheric pressure diminishes in a decreas-
ing ratio as one ascends, and that the
difference between 1,900 and 10,000 is
very much less than that between the
sea level and 1,000 feet.

held session this afternoon

regarding the arbitration treaty in

respect to the Bering Sea. There was

opposition to it. One body of

Senators bitterly resented the idea of

treaty holding the right of the

United States to the waters acquired

rights to the uncertain decision of

treaty would be a distinct gain in

it would commit Great Britain to accept-

ance of the fact that the United

States had no claim to jurisdiction over

the waters of Bering Sea under the

Russian title, a point which she has

steadily refused to allow.

A third group thought that the treaty

should not be approved finally without

the addition of a clause renewing the

modus vivendi. Indeed, there was

manifested a general feeling of dis-

appointment, growing out of the re-

fusal of the British government to re-

spond to the reasonable request of this

government in that respect. Some

Senators took the ground that, while

the treaty might safely be ratified, the

Administration should be instructed in

the event of the continued refusal of

the British government to insure the

protection of the seals during the ar-

bitration proceedings, to order the

vessels of the United States to seize

every offending vessel without regard

to nationality.

After considerable discussion the

treaty was referred to the committee on

foreign relations.


THE CABINET MEETING.

It is understood that the Cabinet has

decided in insist on renewal of the

modus vivendi for the preservation of

seals in Bering Sea.

The Cabinet meeting was important,

notwithstanding the absence of Blaine,

Foster and Noble.

The entire session was devoted to

discussion of the Bering Sea ques-

tion in general. The opinion was

unanimous that the position assumed

by the British government, in oppos-

ing renewal of the modus vivendi,

was untenable and not justified by the

condition of the sealing industry. It

was argued that the opening of Bering

Sea this season to indiscriminate

result in serious injury, if not de-

struction, to the industry, and thus

defeat every objection of the negotia-

tions. It was decided to insist on a

ernment is desirous of reaching a

The State.

The State to-day furnishes some interesting reading on the political situation, which will, no doubt, receive much attention from all factions throughout the State, whether it agrees with their respective views not.

Col. John Z. Haskell, member of the Legislature from Richland county, member of the National Democratic Committee from South Carolina, and one of the most prominent men in politics in the State, returned to the city a few days ago after a stay in New York. Last night he again left for that city on important business. He will return, however, before the meeting of the party committee. It is his resume of the political situation that the State publishes to-day.

We called upon Col. Haskell yesterday and asked for an interview. He found the Colonel "up to his eyes in work, but he consented to give his views on the present political situation. In response to the direct question propounded by the reporter as to what he thought of the political status of affairs in this State, as outlined on the political horizon, he said:

"The political situation, I think, is rather bad. It is very clear that there is a strong opposition to Governor Tillman among the thinking portion of those who supported him two years ago; I believe that good men, if properly supported, could defeat him; but there is a fact which is a very unfavorable sign. The three principal papers of the State, which are all opposed to him, seem as sharp opposed to each other as they are to Tillman, and I fear each paper will have its followers in this antagonism among themselves. I agree fully with the position that we should only fight the evils of the Tillman administration within the party lines. I think any other course is perfectly hopeless. There is no question about it, whether they did it willingly or unwillingly, the majority of those who took part in the last election voted for Tillman. There is no question that however outrageous certain features of the present constitution are (and I think some of them are infamous), it was adopted by a majority of the regular Democratic convention in the State. The people of the South would have been unanimous in pronouncing the Force Bill, if it had passed, as infamous, but that it was no law because it was unjust. I think that, to-day, the party is practically divided, and the question is how to bring it together. It has been divided, not by those who opposed Tillman but by those who followed him. Four years ago the men who since that time have been Tillman supporters inaugurated the outrageous practice of holding secret caucuses during the session of the Legislature and binding the members of the caucus to support those measures. In that way a minority would come into the House with a minority vote, though a large part of their vote, if it had not been bound by the caucus, would have voted with the minority, which was excluded in the caucus.

"A large number were excluded who were not farmers, except those who were obliged to support blindly any measures advocated by the majority of the farmers. Many of the best farmers of the last Legislature were excluded. The call issued recently for the March convention was signed by men who have always voted with the regular Democratic party. Not one of them could have gone into the caucuses which called themselves 'Democratic caucuses.' Such Democrats as Judge Kershaw, Judge Wallace, Senator Butler, General Brittun and many others would not have been eligible to these caucuses, yet this cabal party undertook to absolutely dictate the policy of the party. In other words they said to these gentlemen and other like them: We admit you've been Democrats all your life; you've been most active leaders in the governance of the State; but from this time on we will hold secret oath-bound caucuses, dictate what shall be done, and whether you approve it or not you must follow us.

"The elimination of this was the convention by which a minority in favor of Tillman was converted into an apparent majority for him, and practically turned the State over to a secret oath-bound organization which, by its very terms, excluded men who have been for a generation the accepted leaders of the people. But how long a party can exist when it excludes absolutely from its councils its most distinguished members, it is hard to say. It will be contrary to human nature for men of capacity and character to, for all time, submit to follow the blind dictation of others in measures in which they have no voice. But we cannot lose sight of the fact that the Democratic organization is regular. No matter by what caucusry and tricks the present rulers got control of it, the majority of the people still look on it as the Democratic party and vote within its lines. To break from it or to go against this majority, and to be opposed to this, is a mistake.

"Our only hope, in my opinion, is to awaken the people, who have the right to say who shall be the rulers, to the worthlessness of those who have succeeded in getting into power. To certainly submit and make no opposition because we do not think we will succeed is most cowardly and most foolish; such persons can have no sympathy. I think the letter of Dr. Maxwell comes nearer the mark than anything I have seen; but I think he is wrong—and am sure he will admit it, when he looks into the matter more closely—in saying that the credit of the State and the prices of bonds are not affected by the present administration.

"There is no doubt that the credit of the South generally is seriously affected by the low price of cotton and general depression; but when I remember that the railroads are almost entirely owned by New York capital, some of whom are the leading financiers of New York, it must be self-evident that the attempts to oppress the railroads will be resented by these men. They are the ones who hold southern securities. Our banks depend almost entirely on New York capital for the money with which the business of the country is carried on. New York bankers keep thoroughly posted as to the condition of affairs in this State; and when we see the comptroller, who is recognized as speaking, making attempts which the courts have without dissent pronounced to be illegal attempts at oppression, we find a ready explanation of the fact that New York banks have been very slow to give accommodation to the banks in this State. Insurance companies are among the heaviest lenders of money in the State, and they, too, have felt the oppression of the present administration and resented it.

"I have heard much of these things, as I have been in New York for the last six weeks constantly meeting and conferring with the parties who are most active in Southern enterprises. I believe that the conduct of the courts in enjoined the illegal course of this young man the Comptroller, will have a very happy effect, and nothing will have better effect than the fact that Associate Justice Pope has justified the confidence of his friends, who opposed him politically, in his dignity of the Law.

"I am confident when the people are aroused they will correct these evils themselves. To go outside of the party and try to convert them by attacking them and denouncing them as if they were part of Tillman's government is a great mistake.

"My experience in the last Legislature enables me to say this: The Legislature, with very few exceptions, was composed of strong adherents of Tillman, and with but few exceptions they had no experience in legislative work. Any one who has served in the Legislature knows that a new member waits until he learns the forms, so to speak, and he is liable to be misled. The last Legislature when it came down fell into the hands of Tillman and perhaps the worst set of demagogues who followed him that ever sat within the Halls of the General Assembly."

when you have slapped him on the right

life; as a student he hardly deserves
any recognition, and you have right

corps. The princes of our royal house
have all been corps students in Rome

ceive as members only the highest aris-
tocracy, princes, counts, barons, etc.

NOV. 20, 1892.

The President, like his great predecessor, Abraham Lincoln, never crosses a bridge before he gets to it, and never allows himself to be stampeded by what is printed in sensational newspapers. It may be true, as alleged, that the French Government is, through its agent in Central America, encroaching upon rights claimed by the United States under the Monroe Doctrine, which, as aptly stated by Attorney General Miller, means that no foreign power has the right to interfere with the autonomy of any government upon the Western hemisphere, nor to interfere with the safe conduct of these governments. Foreign powers have not the right, nor will they be allowed, to assume possession of territory or to invoke the aid of arms in interfering with the management of the Panama railroad, which was built by American capitalists; but this government has a minister in Central America for the special purpose of looking after our interests and until his report is made no official notice will be taken of these allegations. By virtue of treaty between the Republic of New Grenada and the United States, which is still enforced and which cannot be affected by any change of ownership in the trans-isthmus railroad, our citizens are given certain rights of traffic on that railroad and those rights will be maintained by this administration, by force if necessary. That's all there is to it.

Senator Chandler will head crusade against immigration at the coming session of Congress, which has for its purpose the shutting out of all immigrants for a period of at least five years. The fight in Congress will be opened when the Joint Senate and House immigration committee shall make its report, upon which it is now working, after spending many months in investigating immigration. The national platform upon which Mr. Cleveland was elected is pledged against further restriction of immigration in these words: "I condemn and denounce any and all attempts to restrict the immigration of the industrious and worthy of foreign lands." But that does not prevent many prominent Democrats agreeing with Senator Chandler that there is need for temporary if not permanent stoppage of immigration.

Death is again lowering over the White House. This time it is Dr. Scott, the aged father of the late Mrs. Harrison, who is awaiting the summons to join his beloved daughter who has so recently gone before. The physicians have informed the President that owing to Dr. Scott's age, he is past ninety-three—there is little or no hope of his recovery from his present illness, which dates from his trip to Indianapolis to see Mrs. Harrison buried. General Rosecrans, who although a Democrat has remained Register of the Treasury ever since he was appointed to that position by Mr. Cleveland, has made himself very solid with the clamorous horde of Democratic office seekers, which has already made its appearance in Washington, by including in his annual report a plea against the working of the Civil Service examination. The rolling of hollow stay bolts is an in
dustry recently introduced and claimed to
possess special advantages, says The Age
of Steel. In this process two pieces of iron
rolled in U-shaped section are laid together
and wired in that position, these parts be-
ing then heated to a welding heat and run
through rolls, and as the welded tube
comes from the rolls it passes over a man
drel, which fills the interior; before reach
ing the second pair of rolls it cools slightly
and shrinks upon the mandrel, and in this
pair of rolls it is drawn from the mandrel
and the interior cleared. In this way, by
five repeated operations, a hollow stay bolt
is obtained which has uniform interior
diameter. The material must necessarily
be the very best quality of charcoal iron;
the bolts are made in lengths of six feet,
and it is alleged that considerable saving
in expense is made by using hollow stay
bolt iron instead of drilling the ends of the
bolts after they are in position

Ambrose Pare, the Famous French Surgeon and His Patent.

Who first invented wooden legs? It is impossible to give an exact and definite answer to the question; but there is some evidence to show that in the sixteenth century a wooden leg was regarded as somewhat of a novelty. One of the most famous surgeons France has ever produced was Ambrose Pare. He was surgeon to several of the French kings, and when, as a protestant, his life was in danger at the time of the St Bartholomew massacre, the king, Charles the ninth, saved him by shutting him up in his own closet. His works, filling great folio, were published towards the end of the sixteenth century, and went through many editions. In the fifth edition, published at Paris in 1593, there is figured a wooden leg which is practically the same as the article in use at the present time, and Pare gives such a very minute description of it that it is only reasonable to conclude that such a continuance was then an unfamiliar object.

The one discovery above all others that has made Pare famous for all time was the plan, which he was the first to suggest, of tying the arteries after the surgical removal of limb. In one part of his writings he gives a curious account of a case of successful amputation, in which he appears to have anticipated one of the latest of modern fads and to have used music as medicine. The patient had been wounded in battle. The famous surgeon took him in hand, successfully amputated the limb, using his new plan of tying the arteries, and when the sufferer began to mend, prescribed what the quaint English of the translation describes as "a consort of violins and a jester to make him merry." In a month the patient was able to hold himself up in chair, and was carried down to the gate of his castle to see the people pass by.

A successful issue to such an operation must have been of rare occurrence, for we are told that the country people of two or three leagues about, knowing they could see him, came the first day, male and female, to sing and dance pell-mell in joy of his amendment, all being very glad to see him, which was not done without good laughing and drinking.

"The camp being broken up," concludes Pare, "I returned to Paris with the gentleman, whose leg I cut off, dressed him and God cured him. I sent him to his house merry with his wounded leg, and was content, saying that he had escaped good cheap not to have been miserably burned."

The success of Pare's comparatively ample and safe mode of procedure, as compared with the barbarous methods formerly in use, which inflicted horrible agony on the sufferer and too often ended in failure, must have led to a considerable growth in the demand for artificial limbs; and the wooden leg, which if not invented by the great French surgeon must certainly have been greatly improved by him, became more frequent adornment of the wounded heroes of those fighting days.

DEAR Mr. Editor: I am not correspondent and have never been contributor to any Newspaper or Journal, but would thank you for small space in your columns.

I suppose everybody in Union County feels interested in the Welfare and progress of their County, and they must admit that the present condition is very gloomy indeed. I think the time has arrived when the different Townships should look to their individual interests and act separately or together, as may seem best, take steps looking to their own advancement and prosperity. It is well known that the Townships of Jonesville and Pinckney already have plans by which they feel sure, if carried out, will institute the beginning of prosperity that will be beneficially felt throughout the length and breadth of Union County.

Everybody in these two Townships know that on Tuesday the 10th inst. is the day appointed for the voters to record their votes for or against subscribing $4,000 each to the capital stock of the Lockhart Shoals Railway, which will run from Jonesville by Kelton to The Shoals, and it is a settled fact, we'll ascertain, that the subscription will be carried by an overwhelming majority.

The writer is informed by a gentleman in a position to know that, the money is already secured ($500,000) to erect the first Cotton Mill at Lockhart Shoals, whenever Railroad transportation to that point is assured, and the most of that amount will come from abroad. Now, Mr. Editor, that amount of money from abroad is no small thing to be dumped down at one time in our stricken County, to say nothing of the $100,000 to come from abroad to complete the Railroad provided the $40,000 in each Township is voted, and am well informed this is just beginning, as every horse power at the Shoals will be utilized, and there is enough power to run 100,000 spindles and accompanying looms.

Did you ever hear, Mr. Editor, of any one, before in the history of Union County, that ever introduced a single dollar of foreign capital into this County, or ever tried to do so? But on the contrary, haven't you correctly heard that many thousands, ($50,000 to $70,000,) have been sent out of the town of Union to Virginia, West Virginia, Tennessee and Kentucky, in the last twelve months, to be placed in the most risky and uncertain investments in the mushroom towns of those States.

The man who will record his vote on the 10th inst. against the Railroad I am proud to say they are very few; should they before doing so, he may have cause to reproach himself in after years, because he will not only be opposing Railroad, but also the building of Cotton Mills and other Manufactories and foreign capital in that way postpone and delay indefinitely that era of prosperity so earnestly wished for and long needed in our poor county. On the contrary, those who will record their votes for these enterprises, especially the young men, and I am told quite a number of them will cast their maiden votes, can, after years, see in the hundreds of thousands of spindles, and looms, fine schools and churches and factory buildings, and several thousands of happy operatives in their comfortable homes at Lockhart Shoals, free from barrooms and other temptations to vice, on proudly say my vote helped to bring about this prosperous state of things.

Mr. Editor, the Townships of Pinckney and Jonesville will have cause to be proud and rejoice at having achieved so much against the vigorous opposition of most of your merchants and some of your prominent Legal fraternity. We can say to the other townships, go and do likewise.

PUBLIC SPIRIT.

The contest is to be a fair, stand up

Prof. A. A. Thompson, geographer in charge of the western division of the United States geological survey, was in the city during the week. He came to inspect the preparations made by Mr. H. T. McKee for starting a topographical survey of Washington in the city next spring. A reporter met the professor and Mr. McKee at the latter's office in the Century Building, and had a most entertaining chat with them.

"The work we are engaged in," said the professor, "is that of making a complete topographical map of the United States under a comprehensive and well-defined plan. These maps are made from original sources of information obtained by accurate surveys made for that purpose. In this respect they differ from ordinary geographic maps, which are usually compiled from secondary sources of information. Many partial surveys have been made under authority of the United States government, but they were conducted by independent organizations without conformity to any general plan, they are of varying degrees of accuracy.

"The most prominent organization, and that which is executing the most accurate work, is the United States Coast and Geodesic Survey, which commenced work in 1882, since when nearly the entire coast line of the Atlantic, Gulf and Pacific has been mapped, together with strip of inshore topography. The United States military engineers have mapped the shores of the great lakes and of the lower Mississippi and Missouri rivers. The war department has also carried on several explorations in the western part of the country. These began with the famous expedition of Lewis and Clarke, which was followed by those of Long, Pike and Fremont. Then followed the Pacific railroad surveys. The surveying methods of these expeditions were crude and their results far from accurate. In 1851 Clarence King made a survey of the country adjacent to the Union and Central Pacific railways. The war department in 1859 undertook extensive surveys in the western mountain region which were discontinued in 1872. The Hayden survey was instituted in 1867, and did work in Montana, Idaho and Yellowstone park, and later in Colorado, Arizona, New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming. The Powell survey originated in 1869 in explorations of the Colorado river, this being the first survey of that stream. In addition to these surveys have been made merely for the purpose of locating state boundary lines, and also surveys of the public lands, which, though they serve admirably their purpose of establishing lines for property reference, possess little topographic value. The post office department also publishes postal route maps, almost wholly by means of compilation. Besides those carried on by the general government, state surveys have been carried on by the governments of New Hampshire, New York, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Kentucky, California and New Jersey.

"The United States geological survey, with which we are connected, is the only organization which has undertaken to map the country under a comprehensive plan, and has surveyed a greater area than any other organization. It was formed in 1879, upon the discontinuance of the three rival Western surveys conducted by Hayden, Wheeler and Powell. The work of topographic surveying on a large scale was commenced in 1882 and has been prosecuted actively since that time. This survey has worked in cooperation with the states of Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut and New Jersey, and has completed the surveys of those states. It has also surveyed large areas in New York, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Virginia, the southern Appalachian region, Louisiana, Texas, Arkansas, Illinois, Iowa, Wisconsin, Missouri, Kansas and the far Western states and territories. Altogether an area of 54,000 square miles has been surveyed by this organization.

"There are about 1,000,000 square miles in the United States, and the government has on hand enough data from various sources to map only 100,000 square miles on a scale of one mile to an inch. On scale of two miles to an inch there is data on hand to map 60,600 square miles, and on scale of four miles to an inch the government could produce maps of 100,000 square miles of its area. This latter area of small scale includes the limited areas of the larger scale. Our survey at first started to map areas on the smaller scale, but the demand for a larger scale was such that we are now making them on a scale of one mile to an inch, except in the mountain regions where the other two scales are also used, the four mile scale however, being nearly obsolete.

"These maps are engraved on copper plates, three being required, one to show the waterways, that are printed in light blue, one to show the contours of elevations printed in brown, and the other to show the artificial features, such as roads, houses, railways, and boundary lines, etc., printed in black. The plates are about sixteen inches square and each plate represents an area of fifteen minutes thirty seconds, or one degree square, according to the scale adopted.

"There is a great and growing demand for these maps which are valuable for many purposes, but the government has made no provision for publishing them. Some 800 map sheets of each map are printed when the plates are first proved and then the plates go into the government vaults to be printed again when congress shall make the necessary appropriation. Many unavailing efforts have been made to induce congress to publish these and sell them for the mere cost of printing a few cents apiece. In many cases the field work necessary for the preparation of one of these maps, fifteen miles square, costs the government as much as 5000. Private map publishers are constantly represented at offices in Washington, and appropriate without cost the work done by the government and charge the public very high prices.

"I have been with Maj. Powell, who is in head of this work, since 1871. I went with him down the canyon of the Columbia river, which was the first expedition to explore that navigable river. We did not see a white man for two months, and many of our adventures were exciting and often thrilling. My present work is that of supervising the work west of the Mississippi river. We have parties in the field in Montana, South Dakota, Nebraska, Colorado, Kansas, Texas, New Mexico, Idaho, South and Central California, Oregon, and are making a beginning in this state. The men spend in about half their time in the field and half in office work. Originally the men used to return to Washington city to do the office work; lately a change has been made in this respect and the policy adopted of opening offices in most prominent and most convenient centers of the districts in which the work is being carried on. This was done for the greater convenience of the men, that they could more readily have access to information possessed by our department. We want to make Mr. McKee's office in this district a distributing center for all the geographic knowledge we possess and a library, not only of our own maps and various others published by the government, but also of all the private state maps of this region which are obtainable. Like all other scientific information, the value of maps depends upon their accuracy, and we want everyone to know that they can here find the most accurate information of this country that is to be obtained, as well as a proper understanding of the relative value of all the various kinds of maps. As for myself, I spend about half my time in the field and half in Washington, and am now going to California, where eight men are doing field work, and from there I shall return to Washington, arriving there about May.

Mr. McKee, who will have charge of the work in this vicinity, very kindly explained the character of the work and the method of making maps at this place.

"This is the first work our survey has taken in this state," said he to the reporter.

LONDON, September 30.--The inhabitants of the Isle of Man were recently thrown into a state of great excitement by a brutal murder committed at Douglas, the principal town of the island. Murder is not often committed on the island, this being the first case that has occurred in seven years.

The victim was Mrs. Edith Ann Cooper, a remarkably pretty woman, about twenty-five years old. She and her husband, George Barker Cooper, a merchant of Manchester, arrived in Douglas in the latter part of August and took rooms at the Regent Hotel. They had been there but a short time when the chambermaid saw the couple quarrelling, and then she heard a slight scream.

The chambermaid testified that she peered through the keyhole in the door of the room occupied by the Coopers and saw Mrs. Cooper, almost nude, lying on the floor. Cooper was kneeling beside her with a towel in his hand.

MURDERED HER AND LIED ABOUT IT.

Cooper subsequently left the room and notified the hotel people that his wife was dead. A constable was summoned and when he entered the room he saw Mrs. Cooper dead on the floor. The policeman saw that the woman had been stabbed, and he asked Cooper whether he had committed the crime. Cooper replied that he did not know, he added that he had been at a bank and when he returned he had found his wife in a faint on the bed. He placed her on the floor and poured water on her, but his efforts to resuscitate her were of no avail.

He afterward said that he must go downstairs and get drink, but the policeman, whose suspicions were aroused, told him that he could not go out of the room. Cooper exclaimed, "I must go," and made for the door, but was stopped by another officer, who had arrived in the meantime.

Cooper was placed under arrest, and as he was led away in custody he exclaimed: "Oh, my God! oh, my God! Let me go back and kiss her before I am taken away!"

HELD FOR TRIAL.

The coroner's jury that examined the case returned a verdict of wilful murder against Cooper and he was held for trial. The case has been proceeding for several days, and the courtroom at Douglas has been crowded with persons from all parts of the Island eager to hear the testimony.

Among the evidence introduced by the prosecution was the nightdress worn by Mrs. Cooper at the time of her death. One of the sleeves had been torn out. A knife with which it is claimed the stabbing had been done was also put in evidence.

The constable who was first summoned testified that the sheets, pillows and bolster on the bed were smeared with blood nearest the side where Mrs. Cooper lay on the floor. The cuffs of the shirt which Cooper was wearing at the time had blood on them. There was blood, too, on the wardrobe floor, and all attempt had apparently been made to wash away the stains, for some towels and handkerchiefs and portion of the deceased's undergarments seemed to have been used to wipe the floor. A garment found under the bed had been used as a mop.

COOPER ALLOWED TO TESTIFY.

Under the Manx law a person accused of a capital crime can be sworn in his own defence, and to-day Cooper was placed in the witness box. A most decided sensation was caused when he confessed that he had had a quarrel with his wife, and that he had killed her by stabbing her with a penknife. He said he did not intend to kill her, but had stabbed her in the heat of passion.

The murdered woman was Cooper's second wife, and they had only been married about a year. About ten years ago Cooper was charged at the Chester Assizes with shooting at his first wife, intending to kill her. The charge arose out of an intrigue in which he had been engaged with a woman named Ditchfield.

He was acquitted, and subsequently his wife secured a divorce from Ditchfield and married again. On the day following the marriage Cooper married the woman whose murder he has now confessed.

MRS. COOPER.

Mrs. Cooper's maiden name was also Cooper, though she was no relation to her husband. She was the daughter of Mr. William Cooper, gentleman of independent means, residing at Shirley. She was highly accomplished and was educated at private schools, Shirley. She was greatly favoured and had a very pleasant disposition. For some reason that has not been explained she took an engagement at the Central Hotel in Douglas; it is believed, she first made acquaintance of Cooper here.

Cooper was a frequent visitor in Douglas, where he was well known and connected. She soon gave up her position in the hotel and went to reside with relatives in London. About eighteen months ago she returned to Shirley and remained at home until her marriage with the man who will now, to all probability, be hanged for killing her.

He said that if Great Britain intended to hold her own in the conflict of commercial treat ies now in progress, she must inflict upon other nations the penalty of refus- ing to let them enter her markets unless they were willing to grant reciprocal fla vors.

 Lord Salisbury also replied at length to the attacks to which he has been sub jected in consequence of his Primrose speech. He had not, he said, urged the men of Ulster to rebel against the Irish Parliament in case of the separation of Ireland and England. He felt, however, with Peel, that the repeal of the union would mean the beginning of a long and bitter religious war in Ireland.

flew away. The female, however, re-

own offspring. On the morning Of the
fourth day the male reappeared accom-
panied by nearly 500 storks, which held
a mass meeting in an adjacent field.

meeting broke up, and all the storks
bounced upon the unfortunate female

them both, and, after. destroying the
polluted nest, took wing and departed
and were never seen there again.-At-
lantic Monthly.

Dakota at Minneapolis, can be mentioned
Hon. D. Haney, of Mitchell, who as a popu-
lar man in his district cannot be excelled.
Judge Haney is the judge of the Fourth dis-
trict and has made an enviable reputation as
Judge and as an eloquent orator. Among
the names offered from Sioux Falls are Mel-
vin Crisby and Hon. H. H. Keith, both of
state renown. Tom Sterling, one of the gal-
lant young republicans of the state, will be
supported by Spink county. Johnson of Cod-
dington and Sheldon of Day are also men-
toned, while Albright of Hughes, Geo.
Matthews of Brookings, Lightmer of Edmunds
and W. H. Smith of Aurora are also men-
toned. C. N. J. Harrison of Huron, who made
such gallant fight for the republicans in the
last house, is another candidate, while Wilson
of Hot Springs, and Martin of Deadwood,
are mentioned as probable Black Hills can-
didates. A number of these men are known
as Pettigrew men, others as Mellette men, al-
though the greater number have not been
identified with any clique and are therefore
peculiarly fitted to represent the state at
Minneapolis.

Time and space are two of the things
which the mind of man can not fully
comprehend. We can not find a start
ing point or a boundary for either so
that when describing the place of any
object or event, we do it by comparing
it with some other place or event with
which the experience of human affairs
has made us all familiar. Thus the

the founding of Rome. We now reck-

Mohammedans from the flight of Mo-
manned.


The Hebrews reckoned twelve lunar
months, or 800 days a year. This being
ten days too small a number of days,
every third year they added another
month. The Romans formerly counted
800 days as a year, with an extra month
inserted at the discretion of the Poti-
fees. In the year B. c. As, Julius Gaze
sar, aided by an astronomer, revised
the Roman calendar. In this revision,
called the Julian calendar, he consid-
cred 365f days as a year. Long after
ward this was found to be eleven min
utes and fourteen seconds too much.
This eleven minutes and fourteen sec.
onds amounts to about nineteen hours
in one century, or to three days in four
centuries. In 1852 this gain had
amounted to ten days, since the general
adoption of the Julian calendar by the
international council at Nice in A. d.
S25. In 1852 Pope Gregory undertook to
correct the error which had caused this
difference of ten days, and to restore
the calendar to the date it would have
borne had the error never existed. He
decreed that October 5, 1852 should be
called October Is. And out of every
four centuries the three century years
which are not divisible by 400 should
not be leap years. This was to pre-
vent future gain of three days out of
every four centuries. AS the gain in
counting time was ten days in 1852, one
century earlier, or in 1899. it was nine
days. October 10, 1902, by the Julian
calendar, would have correspondent to
the time of year represented by Octo-
Der 81 by the Gregorian calendar, the
difference being nine days.


All Catholic countries adopted the
Gregorian calendar at once. Protest
ant England did not adopt it until 1862.
In Russia, the religion of the Greek
Church prevailing, they use the Julian
calendar, which is twelve days behind
the Gregorian. In 1900 it will be thir-
teen days behind, as that is a leap year
according to the Julian calendar, but
not by the Gregorian, which we use.


JOHN T. HENDERSON.

Wordsworth and Scott both celebrated
in their poems the famous old Gelert.
This dog, a deerhound, was given by
King John to his son-in-law Llewellyn,
who kept him at his hunting lodge, in
the neighborhood of the Welsh noun
tain Snowdon. Gelert was missed one
morning from the hunt by his master.
Llewellyn, upon his return to the lodge,
saw the dog, and discovered that its
mouth was besmeared with blood. Con-
Guiding that the dog had devoured his
child. the infuriated master slew the
poor animal. Upon investigation, he
discovered a dead wolf by the child's
cradle, while the child was safely and
soundly sleeping. The brave dog had
saved Llewellyn's heir from the wolf,
A monument was erected to the faithful
creature, which bears the name of Beth
Gelert. .-Harper's Young People.

All the schools gave holiday on Thurs

Mrs. John Williams gave handsome

country home, near Wytheville, on Thurs

Miss Helen Brownleigh gave an informal
dinner party to some of her schoolgirl
friends on Thursday.


Mr. G. N. J. Caldwell, of Bedford, spent

Mr. and Mrs. George Bowers have re-
turned to their home in Washington, to the

Colonel Charles Haller, who has been

weeks, is reported seriously ill to-day. He
has been a citizen of Wytheville for a num-
